---
title: "Same thing, different words"
subtitle: "Your word, the platform's word, and what the difference costs you"
---

Being overwhelmed by the Databricks documentation is very often a vocabulary problem rather than a conceptual one. You know what you are trying to do. You cannot find the page that describes it, because the page uses a different word.

So this works in both directions. If you have a word and need theirs, start below. If you have met one of their words in an error message and need to know what it changes about your work, skip to [the platform's words](#the-platforms-words).

## Your words

These need no explaining, only mapping. In several cases the useful answer is that the platform has no word for the thing, which is worth knowing: it stops you searching.

| Your word | Theirs | Worth knowing |
|----|----|----|
| `sf` object | no equivalent | Geometry is stored as `BINARY` and arrives as bytes you decode yourself. Nothing on the platform holds a geometry column with a CRS attached. |
| CRS, EPSG code | no equivalent | The platform carries an SRID integer on native geometry and nothing at all on `BINARY`. A CRS is yours to keep track of. |
| polygon, raster | geometry, no equivalent | Vector geometry has server-side functions. Raster has none, so `terra` work happens in R. |
| replicate, resample, bootstrap | no equivalent | The platform has no vocabulary for repeats. Searching for one wastes an afternoon: what you want is a page about partitions. |
| fit, tune | no equivalent for your case | Their machine learning vocabulary describes Spark MLlib, not `tidymodels`. It will not help you. |
| `purrr::map()` | no equivalent | The nearest thing is `spark_apply()`, which is a different shape and carries a serialisation cost. See [Run the same simulation on cluster compute](../howdoi/simulate-on-the-cluster.qmd). |
| `furrr`, `future` | no equivalent, and absent | Not installed on the runtime. Base `parallel` is. |
| my laptop | no equivalent, and the point | Nothing on the platform corresponds to "the machine I am sitting at". That distinction is the whole of [What changes when the data is not on your laptop](../concepts/index.qmd). |

A domain noun needs no translation. A catchment is not a Databricks word, and there is no platform term for it to map onto.

## The platform's words

This is where the explaining budget goes. Each entry says what the word means and, more usefully, what it changes about your work.

### Driver

The machine your code runs on unless you have done something specific to send it elsewhere. When you connect from R and call `collect()`, the driver is what you are talking to.

This is the single most load-bearing word on the page, because almost every surprise documented on this site is work happening on the driver when you assumed it was spread out, or the reverse.

### Executor, worker, node

The machines that do work in parallel, as distinct from the one that coordinates. "Worker" and "executor" are used almost interchangeably in Databricks documentation; "node" usually means any machine in the cluster including the driver.

Your cluster may have none of these. A single-node cluster is one machine that is both driver and the only place work can happen, which is ordinary rather than broken. [Work out what the cluster you have can do](../howdoi/compute.qmd) tells you which you have, and it matters more than any other fact about your compute.

### Partition

The unit of parallel work: a chunk of a dataset that one task processes. The count of partitions, and not the count of rows, decides how much runs at once.

That is the consequence worth carrying away. If you split work into four partitions, at most four things happen at a time, however many rows or cores there are. Partition count is the dial, and it is often the only dial you can reach.

### Serialisation

The cost of moving work to another machine: your function, everything it refers to, and the data it needs all have to be converted to bytes, shipped, and rebuilt on the far side.

The counterintuitive consequence, which this site relies on repeatedly: distributing work is not free, so distributing something small can be slower than not distributing it at all. That is not a misconfiguration. It is the cost exceeding the saving.

### Pushdown

Work happening on the server rather than in your session. When you write `dplyr` against a database table and the filter runs inside Databricks, that filter has been pushed down.

This guide mostly says "where the code runs" instead, because that is clearer, but the vendor's word is worth recognising.

### UDF

User-defined function: your own function, run by the platform on data it holds. `spark_apply()` is how you get an R one.

### Volume, DBFS

Storage you can read and write as though it were a filesystem. A Unity Catalog **volume** is the current, recommended form; **DBFS** is the older mechanism, still present and still referenced by a lot of documentation you will find.

A volume appears at `/Volumes/...`, and the qualification matters more than the path: it is a filesystem path **inside a cluster**, not on your machine. From your own R session that path does not resolve, so pointing `readr`, `arrow` or `sf` at it fails with a message that reads like a typo. Fetching a file from a volume into your session is [Read my files from a volume](../howdoi/volume-files.qmd).

Prefer a volume. That is upstream's direction too, not only this guide's judgement: `brickster` deprecated its `db_dbfs_*` functions in 0.2.13, saying explicitly that it is guiding users towards volumes. It is also the answer to most questions about getting a file to where your code runs, which is [Sending things to where your code runs](sending-things.qmd).

### Catalog, schema

Two levels of naming above a table, so a full table name has three parts: `catalog.schema.table`. If you have used `database.table` elsewhere, "schema" is that middle level, and Databricks documentation sometimes uses "database" for it interchangeably.

### Unity Catalog

The governance layer holding catalogs, schemas, tables, volumes and who may see them. Mostly it is the reason a permission error is a permission error rather than a bug, and the reason your tables live at a three-part name.

### Access mode

A property of a cluster deciding, among other things, which languages it will accept. It matters to you because it is narrower than it first appears: a Standard access mode cluster refuses R **notebooks**, while a client connection from your own R session to the same cluster works.

### Cluster lifecycle

That compute starts, runs, goes idle and terminates, and that state is not yours to assume. A cluster you used yesterday is probably stopped today. Starting one takes minutes, not seconds, and nothing shortens that wait.

### Artifact

Anything a run produces that gets stored: a model, a file, a plot. You will meet it in MLflow documentation. For most of what this guide covers, it is a word you can note and move past.

## Where a word means two things

These cost more search time than unfamiliar words do, because you read them confidently and wrongly.

**Worker.** A worker machine in a cluster, or a forked R process inside one machine. Most parallel-R writing means the second; most Databricks writing means the first. That distinction is what separates [Simulate on the cores you have](../howdoi/simulate-locally.qmd) from [Run the same simulation on cluster compute](../howdoi/simulate-on-the-cluster.qmd): the first adds forked processes, the second adds machines.

**Cluster.** A set of machines in Databricks, or in your own vocabulary the output of a clustering algorithm. Rarely confusing in context, but it makes searching for either one noisy.

**Schema.** The middle level of a table name, or the column types of a dataset. Both appear in Databricks documentation, sometimes on the same page.

**Node.** A machine in a cluster, or a vertex in a river network. The second is your word and the collision is accidental, but the river network tables on this site do use it.

**Job.** A scheduled unit of work in Databricks. In ordinary speech, the thing you are trying to get done. When documentation says "job" it means the former, which is a specific object with a definition and a run history.

## Next

If a word sent you here from the middle of something, go back to it. If it was about getting something to the machine your code runs on, that is [Sending things to where your code runs](sending-things.qmd); if it was about the machine itself, see [Work out what the cluster you have can do](../howdoi/compute.qmd).
